title: Against Bo French-ism
author: Charles Fain Lehman
content:
![Against Bo French-
ism](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/11/Screenshot-2026-11-06-at-7.05.12
---AM.png)

Bo French was just one among the many losers in last Tuesday's statewide
Democratic sweep in Texas. French, who was running for a seat on the powerful
Texas Railroad Commission (which regulates the state's oil and gas industry),
had attracted public outrage for an [X
post](https://x.com/bofrench/status/2099118916282810552?ref=compactmag.com) of
a photo of Indian students at a UT Austin football game. "I heard UT
graduation this year looked like this," French wrote. "I didn't believe it.
The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined."

It's unclear whether French's remarks were what cost him his election. Gov.
Greg Abbott lost by roughly the same margin, and Senate nominee Ken Paxton by
nearly twice as much. But all three performed worse than other statewide
Republicans. And French
[measurably](https://x.com/ZacharyDonnini/status/2118427665312940457?ref=compactmag.com)
underperformed in South Asian areas, specifically.

For some, though, the obvious cause of Republicans' comprehensive defeat was
the demographic change that had alarmed French in the first place.
"Demographics is destiny,"
[_wrote_](https://x.com/bennyjohnson/status/2117837045267853613?ref=compactmag.com)
commentator Benny Johnson, noting that Texas is fifty percentage points less
white than it was in 1970. Greg Bovino, the former Border Patrol commander who
led the crackdown in Minneapolis,
[_blamed_](https://x.com/GregoryKBovino/status/2117955884642926646?ref=compactmag.com)
Abbott's loss on votes from H-1B immigrants from India, of whom "70 to 80
percent vote democrat."
[_Other_](https://x.com/BlazeTV/status/2118066341160825215?ref=compactmag.com)
[_pundits_](https://x.com/libsoftiktok/status/2117820571291431187?ref=compactmag.com)
piled on with the same message: Democrats won, in Texas and elsewhere, because
non-white immigrants voted for them overwhelmingly.

The trouble with this argument is not just that it is wrong on the facts,
although it is. Nor is the problem that these influencers are speaking some
forbidden truth. The trouble, rather, is that their theory absolves
Republicans of responsibility for their historic loss. When you blame an
election on the inexorable march of demographic change, you erase the poor
policy choices that caused the electorate to swing wildly against the GOP in
just two years.

> "Their theory absolves Republicans of responsibility for their historic
> loss."

In a much-discussed 2019 [_essay_](https://firstthings.com/against-david-
french-ism/?ref=compactmag.com), Sohrab Ahmari (who would go on to co-found
_Compact_) diagnosed a pathology of the "Never Trump" right that he labeled
"David French-ism," after now-_New York Times_ columnist David French. David
French-ism, in Ahmari's telling, is the compulsive love of principled losing,
a tendency to be a stickler for rules and norms even if and when following
those rules and norms allows the left to run roughshod over America. The
Trump-inspired right, if it stood for anything, was then understood to be
_against_ David French-ism. What mattered was winning.

Today, parts of the post-Trump right have developed their own pathological
love of losing. Call it Bo French-ism. This French-ism has found particular
purchase on the online right, but also influence offline, especially on the
mind of Elon Musk. While Bo French-ism did not cause Republicans' historic
loss, it threatens to cement it, by abandoning the nascent Trump coalition--a
sustainable path forward for the GOP--in favor of the pleasures of pessimism.

Bo French-ism starts with the belief that, as Johnson put it (echoing many
others before him) "demographics is destiny." Devotees divide American
electoral politics into whites (especially white men) who vote for the GOP;
and everyone else, who votes for the Democrats. Thus the inference that, for
example, Republicans' historic loss in Mississippi's and Kansas's senate races
are attributable to demographic change in those states.  
  
Implicit in this view is the idea that turnout, not persuasion, is what drives
elections. To win, Bo French-ists tend to argue, conservatives should play to
(what they believe to be) the base, rather than trying to pull the median
voter into the coalition. Non-white voters' are taken to be not only
Democrats, but inalterably so--they can't have their minds changed. Therefore,
the most important factor is the ratio of white turnout to non-white turnout.  
  
This theory of turnout affects how the new Frenchists think about political
rhetoric. When French himself tweeted his alarm at seeing Indians having fun
at a college football game, he was presumably trying to mobilize a base of
voters who share that sentiment, even at the cost of upsetting Indians. These
are the same people, presumably, that the Department of Homeland Security is
trying to talk to when it
[_promises_](https://x.com/dhsgov/status/2006472108222853298?s=46&t=pdIKPJw2K6wF4XzoU4KArA&ref=compactmag.com)
100 million deportations, or that Bovino was trying to impress with his fancy
[_get-up_](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/01/24/the-problem-with-
greg-bovinos-overcoat-isnt-what-you-think-00745516?ref=compactmag.com) in
Minneapolis. In all of these cases, the goal is either to mobilize the base or
--as often, if not more so--simply
[_signal_](https://www.richardhanania.com/p/the-based-
ritual?ref=compactmag.com) your commitment to principle, even at the expense
of electoral success.  
  
In all of this, the Bo French-ists demonstrate an interesting parallel with
the DSA wing of the Democratic Party. Bernie Sanders Progressives, too, tend
to emphasize turnout over persuasion, arguing that their policy priorities
will mobilize the base even if they alienate the center. As my Manhattan
Institute colleague Jesse Arm has [_noted_](https://www.city-
journal.org/article/manhattan-institute-survey-right-republicans-
gop?ref=compactmag.com), the GOP's activist class is for the first time to the
right of its voters, much as the Democrats' activists have long been to their
voters' left. It's thus no coincidence that the same attitude prevails among
influential parts of both parties: the way to win is to go whole hog on what
they believe.  
  
What's wrong with this theory? Whites do tend to vote for Republicans, while
non-whites do tend to vote for Democrats. But these tendencies are not,
contrary to the French-ists, immutable. That's clear even in the most recent
election. Exit polling
[_finds_](https://x.com/CharlesFLehman/status/2118002438485766384?ref=compactmag.com),
for example, that Latino men swung by 25 points, from voting majority
Republican to voting majority Democrat, in just two years. Nor, for that
matter, are whites an immoveable bloc for the GOP. Democrats won this cycle
with [_the support_](https://circle.tufts.edu/youth-vote-choice-
demographics-2026-midterms?ref=compactmag.com) of young whites generally and
young white men specifically. That's part of the steady
[_loss_](https://x.com/McCormackJohn/status/2118192256721055838?ref=compactmag.com)
of the GOP's support among college-educated whites.

Indeed, such shifting electoral preferences were central to Donald Trump's
victory in 2024. Trump
[_gained_](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2025/06/26/behind-
trumps-2024-victory-a-more-racially-and-ethnically-diverse-voter-
coalition/?ref=compactmag.com) enormous ground among non-white voters of all
stripes,
[_especially_](https://www.tabletmag.com/sections/news/articles/minorities-
moving-right?ref=compactmag.com) non-white men--a gain in turn that's part of
the GOP's longer-term
[_erosion_](https://www.ft.com/content/84b81600-d107-4050-80cf-1d1e276ea54d?ref=compactmag.com)
of Democrats' control of non-white voters. He accomplished this, moreover, not
through racial and ethnic pandering, but through focusing on economic and
culture-war issues where the median voter was aligned with him--rather than
trying to focus on only his base. Ads talking about gender ideology, public
safety, and inflation resonated with median Americans, not just the base, and
helped propel Trump to victory.

Some will object that by criticizing this tendency, I am trying to censor
discussion of the electoral effects of immigration. While I personally dislike
French and others' rhetoric, I also think reasonable people can have concerns
with, and vote to address, the pace of immigration. Failure to recognize the
electorate's legitimate unhappiness with [_11
million_](https://homeland.house.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2025/06/2025-06-10-Green-Brecheen-to-Salas-CHIRLA-re-Federal-
Funding.pdf?ref=compactmag.com) illegal border crossings in four years is part
of how Kamala Harris lost to Donald Trump in 2024.  
  
Nor is it the case that Bo French-ism itself cost Republicans the 2026
midterms. That was plainly the combination of an unpopular war in Iran and
ever-shifting tariffs contributing to the nation's affordability crisis,
compounded by the administration's botched efforts at implementing its
deportation agenda and the president's shady dealings while in an office of
public trust.  
  
However, Bo French-ism is sufficiently influential in certain corners that it
could cause the broader movement to fail to internalize the election's
lessons. It offers a ready-made, ideologically acceptable explanation not only
for what happened, but for why all future elections will probably cash out the
same way. It offers the tempting idea that the GOP doesn't need to learn from
its loss, or try to actually persuade Americans it's worth letting the party
govern again.

There is a narcotic comfort in such complacency. But politics is about
winning. That means assembling a durable majority coalition, including through
persuasion. If Kansas and Mississippi can turn blue in just two years, then
surely anybody's votes are up for grabs. Conservatives should act like it.  
  
The problem with the "zombie Reaganite" right, the Trump right used to say, is
that they prefer losing on principle to winning. The trouble with the Bo
French-ists is that they, too, would prefer to be beautiful losers.
